title: Types of Vector
notes:
Definition

Vectors are classified into several types based on magnitude, direction, and position — unit, null, parallel, equal, negative, collinear, and coplanar vectors.

Examples

  • Unit Vector
  • Null Vector
  • Parallel Vector
  • Equal Vector
  • Negative Vector
  • Collinear Vector
  • Coplanar Vector
examples:
**Q1: How many types of vectors are listed in the notes?**

**Answer:** Seven — unit, null, parallel, equal, negative, collinear, and coplanar vectors.

**Q2: Name all seven types of vectors.**

**Answer:** Unit vector, null vector, parallel vector, equal vector, negative of a vector, collinear vector, coplanar vector.

**Q3: Which vector type has magnitude exactly one?**

**Answer:** Unit vector.

**Q4: Which vector type has magnitude exactly zero?**

**Answer:** Null (zero) vector.

**Q5: Which vector type shares the same direction but can differ in magnitude?**

**Answer:** Parallel vector.

**Q6: Which vector type must match in both magnitude and direction?**

**Answer:** Equal vector.

**Q7: Which vector type has the same magnitude but opposite direction?**

**Answer:** Negative of a vector.

**Q8: Which vector type acts along parallel straight lines?**

**Answer:** Collinear vector.

**Q9: Which vector type lies on the same plane?**

**Answer:** Coplanar vector.

**Q10: Is a unit vector always dimensionless?**

**Answer:** Yes, it purely represents direction.

**Q11: Can a null vector be considered parallel to any vector?**

**Answer:** By convention, yes, since its direction is arbitrary/undefined.

**Q12: How does equal vector differ from parallel vector?**

**Answer:** Equal vectors require the same magnitude too, not just direction.

**Q13: How does negative vector differ from equal vector?**

**Answer:** Negative vectors have same magnitude but opposite (not same) direction.

**Q14: Is every equal vector also a parallel vector?**

**Answer:** Yes, since equal vectors share the same direction, they are automatically parallel.

**Q15: Is every parallel vector also an equal vector?**

**Answer:** No, parallel vectors can have different magnitudes.

**Q16: Is every collinear vector also coplanar?**

**Answer:** Yes, since a line lies within a plane.

**Q17: Is every coplanar vector also collinear?**

**Answer:** No, coplanar vectors need not lie along the same line, just the same plane.

**Q18: Give a real-world example of a unit vector.**

**Answer:** î, ĵ, k̂ representing unit directions along the x, y, z axes.

**Q19: Give a real-world example of negative vectors.**

**Answer:** Action and reaction forces (Newton's third law).

**Q20: Which vector types would you use to describe two ropes pulling in the exact same direction with different force?**

**Answer:** Parallel vectors.

**Q21: Which vector type describes two identical forces acting at the same angle and magnitude?**

**Answer:** Equal vectors.

**Q22: Which vector type is used when defining A − A = 0?**

**Answer:** Null vector.

**Q23: Which vector type is relevant to torque and moment calculations along a beam?**

**Answer:** Collinear (forces along the same line) or coplanar (forces in the beam's plane), depending on setup.

**Q24: Why is classifying vectors into types useful in solving physics problems?**

**Answer:** It helps quickly identify relationships (e.g., resultant behavior, special-case simplifications) between multiple vectors in a system.

**Q25: State two vector types that both involve 'same direction'.**

**Answer:** Parallel vector and equal vector (equal vector additionally requires equal magnitude).

**Q26: State two vector types that both involve zero or maximal special magnitudes.**

**Answer:** Unit vector (magnitude 1) and null vector (magnitude 0).
